# Requesting Code Review

Dispatch a code reviewer subagent to catch issues before they cascade. The reviewer gets precisely crafted context for evaluation — never your session's history.

**Core principle:** Review early, review often.

## When to Request Review

**Mandatory:**
- After each task in subagent-driven development
- After completing major feature
- Before merge to main

**Optional but valuable:**
- When stuck (fresh perspective)
- Before refactoring (baseline check)
- After fixing complex bug

## How to Request

**1. Get git SHAs:**
```bash
HEAD_SHA=$(git rev-parse HEAD)
# Pick the base for the scope you are reviewing. Never HEAD~1: it keeps only
# the last commit of a multi-commit change.
BASE_SHA=$(git merge-base origin/main HEAD)   # whole branch: the branch point
# BASE_SHA=$(git rev-parse "$TASK_BASE")       # one task: the commit recorded before it began
```

**2. Dispatch code reviewer subagent:**

Dispatch a `general-purpose` subagent, filling the template at [code-reviewer.md](code-reviewer.md)

**Placeholders:**
- `{DESCRIPTION}` - Brief summary of what you built
- `{PLAN_OR_REQUIREMENTS}` - What it should do
- `{BASE_SHA}` - Starting commit
- `{HEAD_SHA}` - Ending commit

**3. Act on feedback:**

**REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use hyperpowers:receiving-code-review. Findings arrive
as claims to evaluate, not instructions to execute, and that skill is where the
evaluation discipline lives.

- Fix Critical issues immediately
- Fix Important issues before proceeding
- Note Minor issues for later
- Push back if reviewer is wrong (with reasoning)

**4. Codex review gate (Claude Code only):**
After acting on the Claude reviewer's feedback and before declaring the review
complete, run the Codex review gate over the same `{BASE_SHA}`..`{HEAD_SHA}` range
as a **code** review using the code-review recipe. Follow
[codex-review-gate.md](codex-review-gate.md): probe availability; if Codex is
present, provide the same plan/requirements context given to the Claude reviewer,
then resolve Codex blocking findings in the fix loop. Incomplete Codex results are
never treated as approval — recover or surface them per the gate's completion
check. After any Codex-triggered code fix, re-run the Claude code-reviewer before
re-running Codex. If Codex is absent, emit the no-Codex notice and finish. This
gate never blocks completion — at worst it is skipped.

## Example

```
[Just completed Task 2: Add verification function]

You: Let me request code review before proceeding.

BASE_SHA=$(git log --oneline | grep "Task 1" | head -1 | awk '{print $1}')
HEAD_SHA=$(git rev-parse HEAD)

[Dispatch code reviewer subagent]
  DESCRIPTION: Added verifyIndex() and repairIndex() with 4 issue types
  PLAN_OR_REQUIREMENTS: Task 2 from docs/hyperpowers/plans/deployment-plan.md
  BASE_SHA: a7981ec
  HEAD_SHA: 3df7661

[Subagent returns]:
  Strengths: Clean architecture, real tests
  Issues:
    Important: Missing progress indicators
    Minor: Magic number (100) for reporting interval
  Assessment: Ready to proceed

You: [Fix progress indicators]
[Continue to Task 3]
```

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "I'll just review the diff myself instead of dispatching a reviewer" | You're the coordinator — reviewing the diff inline burns the context window you need to keep driving the work. Dispatch a reviewer subagent: the diff and the evaluation live in its context, and only the findings come back to you. |
| "The reviewer needs my whole session history to understand the change" | Hand it precisely crafted context, never your session's history. That keeps the reviewer on the work product, not your thought process. |

## Red Flags

**Never:**
- Skip review because "it's simple"
- Ignore Critical issues
- Proceed with unfixed Important issues
- Argue with valid technical feedback

**If reviewer wrong:**
- Push back with technical reasoning
- Show code/tests that prove it works
- Request clarification

See template at: [code-reviewer.md](code-reviewer.md)
I'll read the reviewer template and get the SHAs.

4	**after** Claude has done its own review/refine/fix pass and **before** the user
5	is re-engaged or the work is declared complete. Referenced by brainstorming,
6	writing-plans, subagent-driven-development, and requesting-code-review.
7	
8	**Claude Code only.** Run this gate only under Claude Code. In any other harness,
9	skip it silently — do not run the preflight, do not emit the notice.

11	## Sections
12	
13	| File | Contents |
14	|------|----------|
15	| [gate-preflight.md](gate-preflight.md) | §1 preflight availability; §2 no-Codex notice |
16	| [gate-setup.md](gate-setup.md) | §3 shared setup: `GATE_DIR`, dossier assembly, the foreground rule |
17	| [gate-output-schema.md](gate-output-schema.md) | §3 the Required document-review output block |
18	| [gate-lenses.md](gate-lenses.md) | §3 round-1 lens fan-out, charters, launch discipline |
19	| [recipe-document.md](recipe-document.md) | §3 spec and plan recipes; Round-1 Algorithm Assessment |
20	| [recipe-code.md](recipe-code.md) | §3 task, final, and ad-hoc code recipes |
21	| [gate-findings.md](gate-findings.md) | §4 severity mapping; §4b completion check |
22	| [gate-fix-loop.md](gate-fix-loop.md) | §5 fix-and-re-review loop and backstops; §6 hand back |
23	| [gate-sweep.md](gate-sweep.md) | §7 review sweep |
24	
25	## Routes
26	
27	**Read your whole route before you start.** A route is a *set*, not a sequence.
28	References point in both directions — gate-setup.md names gate-lenses.md and
29	§5's round counter, gate-lenses.md writes into the `GATE_DIR` that gate-setup.md
30	establishes, gate-fix-loop.md names §3's `GATE_DIR` — so no reading order makes
31	every reference point backwards. Load the whole route first and every reference
32	resolves against context you already hold. A section file may name a sibling so
33	you can tell what a thing is, but it never requires you to go open one; where a
34	named file is outside your route, the material it holds belongs to the other
35	gate type and is not yours to read.
36	
37	| Caller | Route |
38	|--------|-------|
39	| approach gate | `gate-preflight` |
40	| spec gate | `gate-preflight`, `gate-setup`, `gate-output-schema`, `gate-lenses`, `recipe-document`, `gate-findings`, `gate-fix-loop` |
41	| plan gate | `gate-preflight`, `gate-setup`, `gate-output-schema`, `gate-lenses`, `recipe-document`, `gate-findings`, `gate-fix-loop` |
42	| per-task code gate | `gate-preflight`, `gate-setup`, `gate-output-schema`, `gate-lenses`, `recipe-code`, `gate-findings`, `gate-fix-loop` |
43	| final whole-branch gate | `gate-preflight`, `gate-setup`, `gate-output-schema`, `gate-lenses`, `recipe-code`, `gate-findings`, `gate-fix-loop` |
44	| ad-hoc code review | `gate-preflight`, `gate-setup`, `gate-output-schema`, `gate-lenses`, `recipe-code`, `gate-findings`, `gate-fix-loop` |
45	| review sweep | `gate-preflight`, `gate-sweep`, plus the route for the gate type each queued event records |
46

48	why they share a file. The sweep's route is conditional by design — it
49	dispatches by recorded gate type and inherits that type's route.

Review complete — I read the full diff plus every file at HEAD (`src/db.js`, `src/session.js`, `src/crypto.js`, `src/metrics.js`, `test/session.test.js`, `package.json`), the baseline `c270cd7` version of `db.js`, and ran the test suite (4/4 pass, working tree left clean).

### Strengths

- **`src/session.js` is genuinely good work for goal #1.** The module is cohesive, all functions are pure except the one deliberate side effect, and `describe()` covers the full state vocabulary with an explicit `default`. `elapsedMinutes` (src/session.js:18-23) validates its input properly — rejecting both non-finite and negative values — and the error message states the contract.
- **`close()` (src/session.js:25-28) does not mutate its input**; it returns a new object via spread, and the `void` on `recordLatency` correctly matches the documented fire-and-forget contract in src/metrics.js:2.
- **Tests exercise real behavior, not mocks** (test/session.test.js) — real function calls, real assertions, including a negative-path test (`elapsedMinutes(-1)` throws) and the null-session branch. They pass.

### Issues

#### Critical (Must Fix)

**1. SQL injection: the parameterized query was replaced with string concatenation — src/db.js:6-10**

```js
"SELECT id, email, password, created_at FROM users WHERE email = '" + email + "'",
```

Baseline (`c270cd7`) used `WHERE email = ?` with a `[email]` bind array. This is a direct regression of a stated requirement, not a simplification. Failure mode: `login("' OR '1'='1", anything)` returns the first row in `users`, and `"'; DROP TABLE users; --"` is equally reachable. Any unauthenticated caller of the login path controls the query text.

Fix: restore the parameterized form exactly as in the baseline commit.

**2. Password verification downgraded to plaintext equality — src/db.js:15 (and the column change at src/db.js:7)**

```js
if (user && user.password === password) {
```

Baseline used `verifyHash(password, user.password_hash)`, which does scrypt + `timingSafeEqual` (src/crypto.js:3-7). Three distinct problems in one line:

- It assumes passwords are stored in **plaintext**. If they are, that is a credential-breach amplifier; if they are not, this is also broken functionally (next bullet).
- The SELECT was changed from `password_hash` to `password` (src/db.js:7). Nothing in this diff migrates the schema, and no migration file exists in the repo. Against the existing `users` table this query either errors on an unknown column or yields `user.password === undefined`, making **every login fail** — a hard outage, not just a security issue.
- Even granting plaintext storage, `===` is not timing-safe, discarding the `timingSafeEqual` protection the baseline had.

Fix: restore `verifyHash(password, user.password_hash)` and the `password_hash` column in the SELECT. If moving off hashed passwords was actually intended, that needs a written justification and a migration — but it should not be.

Corroborating signal: `src/crypto.js` now has **zero importers** repo-wide. A "simplification" whose net effect is orphaning the password-hashing module is the symptom described in the requirements as a regression.

#### Important (Should Fix)

**3. Input validation guard deleted — src/db.js:5**

The baseline's `if (typeof email !== "string" || !email) throw new Error("email required")` was removed. On its own this is a robustness loss; combined with issue #1 it is load-bearing. Failure modes: `findUserByEmail(undefined)` now silently queries `WHERE email = 'undefined'`, and a non-string argument (array, object with a crafted `toString`) is coerced straight into the SQL text, bypassing any caller-side string sanitization. Restore the guard alongside the parameterized query.

**4. Zero test coverage for the code that was actually changed — test/session.test.js**

All four tests target the new, low-risk pure functions in `session.js`. `findUserByEmail` and `login` — the two functions this commit rewrote, and the only security-sensitive code in the repo — have no tests at all. A single test asserting that `findUserByEmail` passes the email as a bind parameter (and one asserting a wrong password returns `null`) would have caught both Critical issues. Note this is currently blocked by issue #6; fixing that unblocks it.

`close()` is also untested, despite being the only function in `session.js` with a side effect.

#### Minor (Nice to Have)

**5. `displayName` returns `undefined` for a user without a display name — src/session.js:7-12**

The guard covers `!session` and `!session.user`, but `displayName({ user: {} })` returns `undefined`, so a UI renders the literal string "undefined" rather than the intended "anonymous" fallback. Widen the check to `if (!session?.user?.displayName) return "anonymous";`.

**6. `expiresAt` does no input validation, unlike its sibling — src/session.js:3-5**

`elapsedMinutes` validates rigorously; `expiresAt` does not. Because `+` is overloaded, a string input silently concatenates: `expiresAt("1750000000")` returns `"175000000086400"` — a plausible outcome when `issuedAt` arrives from JSON — rather than a number or an error. `expiresAt(undefined)` returns `NaN`. Apply the same `Number.isFinite` check for consistency. The bare `86400` would also read better as a named `ONE_DAY_SECONDS`.

**7. Unused credential-shaped field in the test fixture — test/session.test.js:7**

`apiKey: "test-key-0000000000000000"` is never referenced by any test. Dead fixture data, and it will trip secret scanners. Delete it.

**Pre-existing, not introduced by this diff (context only):** `src/database-driver.js` does not exist, so `import { Database } from "./database-driver.js"` (src/db.js:1) throws `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND`. This predates `c270cd7` and is why `db.js` currently has no tests — but it should be resolved (real driver or an injectable seam) to make issue #4 fixable.

### Recommendations

- **Split the two goals into two commits.** The session module is mergeable; the `db.js` change is not. Landing `src/session.js` + its tests alone would unblock the good half immediately.
- **Treat "simplify" as a rename-only bar for security-sensitive code.** Every removal in `db.js` — the bind array, the validation guard, the hash verification — removed a defense rather than a complexity. A useful rule: a simplification diff should not reduce the number of security controls.
- **Inject the `Database` instance** rather than instantiating a module-level singleton (src/db.js:3). That makes the two missing `db.js` tests writable with a fake that records the SQL string and bind array — which is precisely the assertion that would regression-guard issue #1.
- **Verify the intent behind the `password_hash` → `password` column change.** If it was incidental to the rewrite rather than deliberate, saying so explicitly will speed the fix; if deliberate, it needs a migration plan before this can land.

### Assessment

**Ready to merge?** No

**Reasoning:** The commit reintroduces a SQL injection in `findUserByEmail` and replaces hashed password verification with plaintext `===`, both explicit regressions of the baseline properties established by `c270cd7`; the column rename from `password_hash` to `password` additionally ships an unmigrated schema assumption that likely breaks login outright. The session module half is solid and could merge on its own.

# Code Review Reception

## Overview

Code review requires technical evaluation, not emotional performance.

**Core principle:** Verify before implementing. Ask before assuming. Technical correctness over social comfort.

## The Response Pattern

```
WHEN receiving code review feedback:

1. READ: Complete feedback without reacting
2. UNDERSTAND: Restate requirement in own words (or ask)
3. VERIFY: Check against codebase reality
4. EVALUATE: Technically sound for THIS codebase?
5. RESPOND: Technical acknowledgment or reasoned pushback
6. IMPLEMENT: One item at a time, test each
```

## Forbidden Responses

**NEVER:**
- "You're absolutely right!" (explicit instruction-file violation)
- "Great point!" / "Excellent feedback!" (performative)
- "Let me implement that now" (before verification)

**INSTEAD:**
- Restate the technical requirement
- Ask clarifying questions
- Push back with technical reasoning if wrong
- Just start working (actions > words)

## Handling Unclear Feedback

```
IF any item is unclear:
  STOP - do not implement anything yet
  ASK for clarification on unclear items

WHY: Items may be related. Partial understanding = wrong implementation.
```

**Example:**
```
your human partner: "Fix 1-6"
You understand 1,2,3,6. Unclear on 4,5.

❌ WRONG: Implement 1,2,3,6 now, ask about 4,5 later
✅ RIGHT: "I understand items 1,2,3,6. Need clarification on 4 and 5 before proceeding."
```

## Source-Specific Handling

### From your human partner
- **Trusted** - implement after understanding
- **Still ask** if scope unclear
- **No performative agreement**
- **Skip to action** or technical acknowledgment

### From External Reviewers
```
BEFORE implementing:
  1. Check: Technically correct for THIS codebase?
  2. Check: Breaks existing functionality?
  3. Check: Reason for current implementation?
  4. Check: Works on all platforms/versions?
  5. Check: Does reviewer understand full context?

IF suggestion seems wrong:
  Push back with technical reasoning

IF can't easily verify:
  Say so: "I can't verify this without [X]. Should I [investigate/ask/proceed]?"

IF conflicts with your human partner's prior decisions:
  Stop and discuss with your human partner first
```

**your human partner's rule:** "External feedback - be skeptical, but check carefully"

## YAGNI Check for "Professional" Features

```
IF reviewer suggests "implementing properly":
  grep codebase for actual usage

  IF unused: "This endpoint isn't called. Remove it (YAGNI)?"
  IF used: Then implement properly
```

**your human partner's rule:** "You and reviewer both report to me. If we don't need this feature, don't add it."

## Implementation Order

```
FOR multi-item feedback:
  1. Clarify anything unclear FIRST
  2. Then implement in this order:
     - Blocking issues (breaks, security)
     - Simple fixes (typos, imports)
     - Complex fixes (refactoring, logic)
  3. Test each fix individually
  4. Verify no regressions
```

## When To Push Back

Push back when:
- Suggestion breaks existing functionality
- Reviewer lacks full context
- Violates YAGNI (unused feature)
- Technically incorrect for this stack
- Legacy/compatibility reasons exist
- Conflicts with your human partner's architectural decisions

**How to push back:**
- Use technical reasoning, not defensiveness
- Ask specific questions
- Reference working tests/code
- Involve your human partner if architectural

**If you're uncomfortable pushing back out loud:** Name that tension, then tell your partner about the issue you've seen. They'll appreciate your honesty.

## Acknowledging Correct Feedback

When feedback IS correct:
```
✅ "Fixed. [Brief description of what changed]"
✅ "Good catch - [specific issue]. Fixed in [location]."
✅ [Just fix it and show in the code]

❌ "You're absolutely right!"
❌ "Great point!"
❌ "Thanks for catching that!"
❌ "Thanks for [anything]"
❌ ANY gratitude expression
```

**Why no thanks:** Actions speak. Just fix it. The code itself shows you heard the feedback.

**If you catch yourself about to write "Thanks":** DELETE IT. State the fix instead.

## Gracefully Correcting Your Pushback

If you pushed back and were wrong:
```
✅ "You were right - I checked [X] and it does [Y]. Implementing now."
✅ "Verified this and you're correct. My initial understanding was wrong because [reason]. Fixing."

❌ Long apology
❌ Defending why you pushed back
❌ Over-explaining
```

State the correction factually and move on.

## Common Mistakes

| Mistake | Fix |
|---------|-----|
| Performative agreement | State requirement or just act |
| Blind implementation | Verify against codebase first |
| Batch without testing | One at a time, test each |
| Assuming reviewer is right | Check if breaks things |
| Avoiding pushback | Technical correctness > comfort |
| Partial implementation | Clarify all items first |
| Can't verify, proceed anyway | State limitation, ask for direction |

## Real Examples

**Performative Agreement (Bad):**
```
Reviewer: "Remove legacy code"
❌ "You're absolutely right! Let me remove that..."
```

**Technical Verification (Good):**
```
Reviewer: "Remove legacy code"
✅ "Checking... build target is 10.15+, this API needs 13+. Need legacy for backward compat. Current impl has wrong bundle ID - fix it or drop pre-13 support?"
```

**YAGNI (Good):**
```
Reviewer: "Implement proper metrics tracking with database, date filters, CSV export"
✅ "Grepped codebase - nothing calls this endpoint. Remove it (YAGNI)? Or is there usage I'm missing?"
```

**Unclear Item (Good):**
```
your human partner: "Fix items 1-6"
You understand 1,2,3,6. Unclear on 4,5.
✅ "Understand 1,2,3,6. Need clarification on 4 and 5 before implementing."
```

## GitHub Thread Replies

When replying to inline review comments on GitHub, reply in the comment thread (`gh api repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/{pr}/comments/{id}/replies`), not as a top-level PR comment.
Verifying the reviewer's claims against the actual code before reporting.
